To gambol means to run, jump, and move about in a light, playful, and carefree way — purely for the sheer joy of moving. There is no purpose behind it, no destination, and no urgency. The creature that gambols is simply happy, and its body is expressing that happiness through free, bouncy, energetic movement.

Think of a young lamb on a spring morning, leaping and bounding across an open meadow for no reason other than that it feels wonderful to do so. That is gambaling in its purest form.

What makes gambol special is the emotional quality it carries. It isn't just any kind of jumping or running. Every time this word is used, it brings with it three things:

Lightness — the movement feels airy, not heavy or clumsy.
Joy — it is always happy movement, never frantic or afraid.
Freedom — nothing is forcing it; it happens naturally and spontaneously.

If you strip away any one of these three things, the word no longer fits. A frightened cat leaping away is not gambaling. A soldier jumping over an obstacle is not gambaling. But a puppy bouncing in circles around its owner for no reason? That is gambaling perfectly.

The word is most naturally and commonly used for:

  • Young animals — lambs, foals, puppies, kittens, calves. In fact, the image of lambs gambaling in a field is so classic that it has almost become the default picture the word paints.
  • Children — playing freely, without a care, running around a garden or a park.
  • Adults — rarely, and usually in a poetic or playful context.

The reason young animals and children dominate this word is that gamboling is deeply tied to innocence. It is the kind of movement that belongs to creatures who have not yet learned to be worried about anything.

• The lambs gamboled across the hillside in the warm afternoon sun.
  • The children gamboled through the sprinklers, shrieking with delight.
  • A pair of young deer gamboled at the edge of the forest, chasing each other between the trees.
  • The foals had been stiff and shy at first, but within an hour they were gamboling freely around the paddock.

Notice that in every example, the movement is happy, light, and purposeless in the best possible sense.

(A quick spelling note: you may see it written as gamboled/gamboling in American English or gambolled/gambolling in British English. Both are correct.)

This is important for sharpening your understanding:

  • It is not purposeful movement. Running to catch a bus, chasing prey, or jumping to reach something — none of these are gambaling, because they all have a goal.
  • It is not slow or calm. Gambaling has energy and bounce. A cat lazily stretching is not gambaling.
  • It is not rough or aggressive. Even when puppies play-wrestle, the word gambol refers to the light, leaping, bounding parts of their play — not the tumbling or biting.
  • It is not clumsy or awkward. There is a natural grace to it, even if it looks silly.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Frolic is the closest word to gambol, and the two are often interchangeable. The small difference is that frolic can describe playful behavior more broadly (including laughter, jokes, and fun), while gambol is more specifically tied to the physical act of light, leaping, bounding movement.

Skip refers to one specific repeated motion (the hop-step pattern). Gambaling can include skipping, but it is a broader, messier, more spontaneous mix of leaps and bounds — not a single defined motion.

Prance involves high, deliberate, showy steps — think of a horse lifting its knees elegantly. Gambaling is far less controlled and deliberate than prancing. It is wilder and more joyful.

Romp is boisterous, energetic play that tends to be louder and rougher. Gambaling is lighter and more graceful by comparison.
Register: Where Will You See This Word?

Gambol is a literary and somewhat old-fashioned word. You will encounter it far more often in novels, poetry, and nature writing than in everyday conversation. It has a warm, gentle, almost whimsical feeling to it. When a writer chooses gambol instead of play around or frolic, they are usually painting a picture deliberately — evoking innocence, open fields, spring mornings, and unbothered young creatures.

In casual speech, most people would just say "the puppies were running around playing" or "the kids were frolicking." But when a writer reaches for gambol, they want you to see the lightness of it — the little leaps, the mid-air turns, the pure physical joy. The word is doing extra work, and it does that work beautifully.
To gambol is to leap and bound about playfully, with lightness and joy, for no reason other than the pure delight of moving.
